topic_title: Federal Structure: Union-State Relations, Governor's Role, Seventh Schedule & Devolution Challenges
syllabus_mapping: Functions and Responsibilities of the Union and the States, Issues and challenges pertaining to Federal Structure: Devolution of Power and Finances up to local levels and Challenges therein. Role of Governor in States - Distribution of powers between the Union and States (Union list, State list and Concurrent list).

content.text: Indian Federalism: Union-State Relations, Institutional Friction, Seventh Schedule, and Fiscal Devolution

Article 1(1) of the Indian Constitution defines India as a 'Union of States'. Described by K.C. Wheare as 'quasi-federal' and by Granville Austin as 'cooperative federalism', the Indian federal model incorporates an indestructible Union with destructible States (Article 3), exhibiting structural central bias ('unitary tilt') while distributing legislative, administrative, and financial powers under Part XI and Part XII.

content.caption: The Threefold Distribution of Legislative Competence under Article 246
rows: Matters of national importance: Defense, Armed Forces, Foreign Affairs, Atomic Energy, Banking, Insurance, Currency & Coinage, Railways, Major Ports, Inter-State Trade.
Matters of local/state concern: Public Order, Police, Public Health and Sanitation, Prisons, Agriculture, Local Government, Markets & Fairs, Tolls, Land Revenue.

Criminal Law & Procedure, Civil Procedure, Marriage & Divorce, Forests (transferred by 42nd Am.), Education (42nd Am.), Protection of Wild Animals (42nd Am.), Weights & Measures (42nd Am.), Trade Unions, Price Control.
Vested exclusively in Parliament (Art. 248 & Entry 97 List I)
Matters not enumerated in any of the three lists (e.g., Cyber Laws, Space exploration, Disaster Management) fall strictly under Union legislative competence.

content.text: Doctrinal Safeguards: (1) Doctrine of Territorial Nexus (Art. 245); (2) Doctrine of Pith and Substance (examining the true nature of a statute when competence overlaps, State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara); (3) Doctrine of Colorable Legislation ('What cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly'); (4) Repugnancy under Article 254 (Union law prevails over State law in Concurrent List unless State law received Presidential assent).
2. Exceptional Parliamentary Inroads into the State List

items: National Interest Resolution by Rajya Sabha (Article 249): Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by a 2/3rd majority of members present and voting declaring that it is necessary in national interest.
National Emergency (Article 250): Parliament gains concurrent power to legislate on any State List subject during an active proclamation under Article 352.

Agreement by Two or More States (Article 252): When legislatures of two or more states pass resolutions requesting Parliament to enact a law on a State subject (e.g., Prize Competitions Act, Water Pollution Act).
Implementation of International Treaties (Article 253): Parliament can enact legislation on any subject to implement international agreements (e.g., TRIPS, environmental protocols).
President's Rule (Article 356): Powers of the State Legislature are declared exercisable by or under the authority of Parliament.

content.text: 3. The Role of Governor: Flashpoints and Judicial Interventions

Appointed by the President under Article 155 during pleasure (Article 156), the Governor holds a dual role: constitutional head of the State executive and representative of the Union Government. Several flashpoints have arisen regarding discretionary authority:

content.caption: Key Constitutional Flashpoints Regarding the Office of Governor
rows: Historically weaponized to dismiss elected opposition state governments. Landmark S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) judgment subjected Article 356 proclamations to judicial review, mandate floor test as the sole criterion for majority, and prohibited dissolution of legislative assembly until parliamentary approval.

Governors withholding assent indefinitely on bills passed by State Assemblies. In State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor (2023), the Supreme Court ruled that a Governor cannot sit indefinitely on bills; if assent is withheld, the bill must be returned 'as soon as possible' to the legislature.
Discretionary reservation of state legislation (mandatory only if derogating High Court powers); often used to stall progressive state laws.
Arbitrary discretion in inviting leaders. Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions recommended inviting: (1) Pre-poll alliance, (2) Single largest party, (3) Post-poll alliance with majority.

content.caption: The Supreme Court of India in New Delhi, the constitutional arbiter of federal disputes under Article 131, which delivered landmark federalism judgments in S.R. Bommai and the Punjab Governor cases.

content.text: 4. Inter-State Federal Bodies & Commissions on Centre-State Relations

items: Inter-State Council (Article 263): Established on the recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission via Presidential Order in 1990; chaired by the Prime Minister; includes all Chief Ministers and Union Cabinet Ministers to investigate and discuss matters of common federal interest.

Zonal Councils (States Reorganisation Act 1956): Statutory deliberative bodies (Northern, Central, Eastern, Western, Southern - AP belongs to Southern Zonal Council) chaired by the Union Home Minister to foster regional cooperation.

Sarkaria Commission Recommendations (1983–1988): Advocated that Article 356 be used only as an extreme 'measure of last resort'; consultation with Chief Minister prior to appointing the Governor; active consultation on Concurrent List legislation; permanent activation of the Inter-State Council.

M.M. Punchhi Commission Recommendations (2007–2010): Recommended fixed 5-year tenure for Governors; removal of Governors only through an impeachment process by the State Legislature mirroring Presidential impeachment; amendment of Articles 355 and 356 for 'localized emergency' without toppling state governments; structured guidelines on pocket vetoes under Article 200.

content.text: The introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act (2016) created a dual unified indirect tax architecture administered by the GST Council (Article 279A). While unifying national markets, it surrendered significant autonomous indirect taxation powers of States:

items: Cesses and Surcharges Proliferation: Union cesses and surcharges (e.g., Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess, Road & Infrastructure Cess) do not form part of the divisible tax pool under Article 270, shrinking the actual net divisible pool shared with States.
Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS): High state co-funding burdens (typically 60:40 or 50:50) distort State fiscal priorities and constrain discretionary capital expenditure.

Borrowing Restrictions (Article 293(3)): Union Finance Ministry restrictions capping Net Borrowing Ceilings (NBC) and adjusting extra-budgetary borrowings by State public sector corporations against the state's fiscal deficit quota.

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Critically examine the role and constitutional position of the Governor as an agent of the Centre versus the constitutional head of the State. Cite relevant recommendations of the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Introduce dual role under Articles 153-163; discuss constitutional friction areas (discretion under Article 200 on State Bills, subjective reports triggering Article 356, appointment of Chief Ministers in fractured mandates); detail S.R. Bommai (1994) and Punjab/Telangana Governor rulings (2023); synthesize recommendations: Sarkaria (appointing eminent persons detached from local active politics, prior consultation with CM) and Punchhi (impeachment by State Assembly, fixed 5-year tenure); conclude on establishing constitutional morality over partisan loyalty.

Discuss the impact of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) and the proliferation of non-divisible cesses/surcharges on Indian fiscal federalism. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Explain structural transformation under 101st Amendment (subsuming state VAT/entry tax into dual GST); analyze loss of state fiscal autonomy; examine Article 270 carve-out allowing Union to retain cesses and surcharges without devolution, reducing effective tax devolution below the 41% recommended by the 15th Finance Commission; evaluate the dispute settlement mechanism and voting parity in the GST Council (Union holding 1/3rd veto weightage); conclude with reform proposals (bringing cesses into divisible pool, formula-based devolution).

Explain the distribution of legislative subjects between the Union and the States under the Seventh Schedule. Under what exceptional circumstances can Parliament legislate on items in the State List? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Frame Article 246 (Union, State, Concurrent Lists) and Article 248 (residuary powers in Parliament); explain judicial doctrines (Pith and Substance, Repugnancy under Art. 254); detail the 5 exceptional situations empowering Parliament over State List: Article 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution in national interest), Article 250 (National Emergency), Article 252 (consent of two or more states), Article 253 (international treaties), and Article 356 (President's Rule).

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. Which Article of the Indian Constitution empowers the Rajya Sabha to authorize Parliament to legislate on a matter in the State List in national interest?
(a) Article 248
(b) Article 249
(c) Article 250
(d) Article 252
Correct Answer: (b) Article 249 [Explanation: Under Article 249, if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting, Parliament can enact laws on any State List matter for up to one year.]

Q2. The landmark 9-judge constitutional bench judgment of the Supreme Court that subjected the imposition of President's Rule under Article 356 to strict judicial review was:
(a) Golaknath v. State of Punjab
(b) S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
(c) Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
(d) Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Correct Answer: (b) S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) [Explanation: In S.R. Bommai (1994), the Supreme Court ruled that secularism is a basic feature, the Governor's proclamation is subject to judicial review, and the floor of the Assembly is the only place to test majority.]

Q3. The Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations submitted its comprehensive report in which year?
(a) 1983
(b) 1988
(c) 1993
(d) 2000
Correct Answer: (b) 1988 [Explanation: Appointed in 1983 under the chairmanship of Justice R.S. Sarkaria, the commission submitted its seminal report on Centre-State relations in 1988.]

Q4. Which Constitutional Amendment transferred five subjects (including Education, Forests, and Protection of Wild Animals) from the State List to the Concurrent List?
(a) 24th Amendment Act, 1971
(b) 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
(c) 44th Amendment Act, 1978
(d) 52nd Amendment Act, 1985
Correct Answer: (b) 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 [Explanation: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976 transferred five subjects—Education, Forests, Weights and Measures, Protection of Wild Animals and Birds, and Administration of Justice (below High Courts)—from the State List to the Concurrent List.]

Q5. Under Article 279A, the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council is chaired by:
(a) Prime Minister of India
(b) Governor of RBI
(c) Union Finance Minister
(d) Union Cabinet Secretary
Correct Answer: (c) Union Finance Minister [Explanation: Article 279A(2) designates the Union Finance Minister as the Chairperson of the GST Council, with State Finance/Taxation Ministers as members.]
